chapter.title: The bell that starts the line

cards.body:
Every workflow is a small assembly line, and **nothing on the line moves until a bell rings**. Picture a bakery at 6 a.m.: the alarm goes, and only then do the ovens light and the trays start sliding down the belt.

In n8n that bell is the *trigger*, the first box on the canvas. It is the only kind of box that can start a run.
cards.simpler: Think of a workflow as a small assembly line. **Nothing on the line moves until a bell rings.** Imagine a bakery at 6 a.m. The alarm sounds, and only then do the ovens turn on and the trays start moving along the belt. In n8n, that bell is called the trigger. It is the first box on the canvas, and it is the only kind of box that can start a run.

cards.prompt: Priya wants this: 'every weekday at 6 a.m., send the baker a reminder to preheat the ovens.' Which part is the bell that starts the line?

whyNot.a: That's a station, not the bell: the message is a job done after the line has already started.
whyNot.c: That's what happens after the line finishes: the workflow never even knows the baker read it.

cards.reteach: The bell is the event that happens first, before n8n does anything at all. Ask: what has to happen in the world for this to begin? Here, the clock reaching 6 a.m. is that event. Everything after it is work on the belt.

cards.title: The first box is always a bell
cards.body:
First, get in. Sign up for n8n Cloud in the browser, or if your laptop has Node installed, type *npx n8n* in a terminal and open localhost:5678.

A new workflow is a blank canvas with one button: add first step. **Every choice it offers is a trigger**, a box that waits for one event and then wakes the workflow. Nothing else may go first.

The simplest bell is the *Schedule Trigger*. You pick how often: every minute, every day at 9, every Monday. When the clock hits that time, the bell rings and one run starts.
cards.simpler: Sign up for n8n Cloud in your browser, or if your laptop has Node, type npx n8n in a terminal and open localhost:5678. A new workflow is a blank canvas with one button: add first step. **Every choice it offers is a trigger**, a box that waits for one event and then wakes the workflow. The simplest is the Schedule Trigger. You pick how often, such as every Monday. When that time comes, the bell rings and one run starts.

cards.title: Marta and the fridge
cards.body:
Marta runs an office of 12 people and is tired of the shared fridge. She builds a Schedule Trigger set to weekdays at 08:45, then a node that writes the message 'Fridge clean-out is Friday. Yes, that yoghurt too.' For 3 weeks the fridge is spotless.

Then a public holiday lands on a Monday. At 08:45 the bell rings anyway, and the message goes out to an empty office. **The clock does not know about holidays.** It only knows the time you gave it.
cards.simpler: Marta runs an office of 12 people and is tired of the shared fridge. She sets a Schedule Trigger for weekdays at 08:45, then adds a node that writes: 'Fridge clean-out is Friday. Yes, that yoghurt too.' For 3 weeks it works. Then a holiday falls on a Monday. At 08:45 the bell rings anyway, and the message goes out to an empty office. **The clock does not know about holidays.** It only knows the time you gave it.

cards.prompt: Dev sets a Schedule Trigger to every Monday at 09:00. It is Wednesday at 3 p.m. and he wants to see the run happen now. What should he do?

options.text: Press the Test workflow button at the bottom of the canvas
Delete the trigger so the workflow runs freely

whyNot.a: That's waiting for the real bell: a test run rings it for you, right now, whatever the schedule says.
whyNot.c: That's removing the bell, not ringing it: with no trigger the workflow can never start at all.

cards.reteach: A test run is you pressing the bell by hand. n8n ignores the schedule, starts one run immediately, and shows you what each box produced. The schedule only matters later, once the workflow is switched on.

cards.title: Ringing the bell by hand
cards.body:
A trigger set to Monday at 9 will not ring on a Wednesday. So while you build, you press the run button at the bottom of the canvas, labelled *Test workflow* or *Execute workflow* depending on your version. **A test run rings the bell for you, right now**, whatever the schedule says.

Marta's story showed the other half. The bell is dumb on purpose. It knows one event and nothing else: not holidays, not whether anyone is in. Deciding those things is work for stations further down the belt, in later chapters.

And a schedule only rings on its own once the workflow is switched on. Until then it waits for your finger. Chapter 7 has the switch.
cards.simpler: A Monday trigger will not ring on a Wednesday. So while you build, you press the run button at the bottom of the canvas, called Test workflow or Execute workflow. **A test run rings the bell for you, right now**, whatever the schedule says. The bell is dumb on purpose. It knows one event, not holidays or who is in. A schedule only rings by itself once the workflow is switched on. Chapter 7 has the switch.

cards.body: Sam drags a Slack node onto the canvas, writes a message, saves, and waits. Nothing happens for 2 days. He has built a station with no bell: there is no trigger box, so no event can start the line. You can spot it at a glance: **a trigger node shows a small lightning bolt** on its left edge, and if your leftmost box has no bolt, add a trigger in front of it.
cards.simpler: Sam drags a Slack node onto the canvas, writes a message, saves, and waits. Nothing happens for 2 days. He has built a station with no bell. There is no trigger box, so no event can start the line. You can spot this at a glance: **a trigger node shows a small lightning bolt** on its left edge. If your leftmost box has no bolt, add a trigger in front of it.

cards.prompt: A workflow has a Schedule Trigger set to 07:00 daily, and the workflow is not switched on yet. Which sentence is true?

options.text: It runs at 07:00 tomorrow by itself
It runs only when you press the test button, until it is switched on
It runs once, right now, because you saved it

whyNot.a: That's the behaviour after switching on: an off workflow's clock is not ticking yet.
whyNot.c: That's a test run, not saving: saving stores the plan, it never rings the bell.

cards.reteach: There are two ways to ring the bell. Your finger on the test button works any time. The clock only works once the workflow is switched on. Saving is neither; it just keeps your drawing of the line.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Every n8n workflow starts with one trigger, the bell that waits for a single event like a time of day and then starts a run. **While building, you ring it yourself with the test button**; the clock only rings it on its own once the workflow is switched on.
cards.simpler: Every n8n workflow starts with one trigger. That is the bell. It waits for a single event, like a time of day, and then starts a run. **While building, you ring it yourself with the test button.** The clock only rings it on its own once the workflow is switched on.

cards.body: Open n8n, add a Schedule Trigger, then an Edit Fields node with one field named message and the value 'Coffee time'. Press Test workflow and watch the words appear in the output panel.
cards.simpler: Open n8n and add a Schedule Trigger. Then add an Edit Fields node with one field. Name the field message and give it the value 'Coffee time'. Press Test workflow. **Watch the words appear in the output panel.** That is your first bell, rung by hand, starting your first run.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now build a workflow that wakes on a schedule, ring its bell by hand, and watch it do one visible thing.
